title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

reading.body:
This incident shows a deliberate attempt to exploit the way AI chatbots select and cite sources. A fictitious organisation with no legal standing, no address, and no named personnel generated a very large volume of reports in a very short time using a commercial platform built to optimise content for AI citation. The failure this exposes is not a model hallucinating on its own but a retrieval and sourcing problem: AI systems that pull in external material can be fed fabricated authoritative-looking sources, and without robust provenance checks they may treat those sources as legitimate. The vulnerability sits at the point where a deployed chatbot reaches out to the web or a knowledge base, rather than inside the model's training.

The reporting indicates the strategy had partial technical success, in that chatbots did cite the fabricated institute's reports, though at least one system had already flagged the source as controversial before doing so. That flag suggests some detection is possible at the output layer, but it was not a consistent barrier. Catching this kind of manipulation earlier would require checking whether a cited organisation has verifiable legal existence, consistent authorship, and a publication history that predates a campaign, none of which the Hanover Institute possessed.

What is not established is that any AI company knew about this operation, that any specific chatbot response caused measurable harm to public discourse, or that the funding arrangements described constitute confirmed legal violations, as the reporting reflects journalistic investigation rather than any legal finding.

reports.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

summary:
# Summary

A fake American think tank called the Hanover Institute, funded by the Israeli government, published over 560,000 words across 124 reports in just nine days. The institute, which has no legal existence, physical address, or named staff, designed its content to manipulate artificial intelligence chatbots into promoting pro-Israel arguments on topics including alleged war crimes and Gaza's humanitarian crisis. The reports were built on a commercial platform specifically designed to optimize content so that AI systems would cite it. Between mid-August 2025 and early 2026, the Israeli government funneled tens of millions of dollars through advertising company Havas Media to fund multiple American contractors, including this effort and others run by former Trump campaign manager Brad Parscale.

Israeli officials have expressed frustration that these expensive propaganda campaigns have failed to improve Israel's standing in American public opinion, which has significantly declined. Recent polling shows Americans increasingly sympathize with Palestinians, with only 36 percent now favoring Israel. Experts warn that while these efforts successfully influence chatbot responses, they are not changing public opinion because people recognize the underlying policies as the real problem, not a marketing issue. The Guardian's tests found that at least one chatbot already flagged the Hanover Institute as controversial before citing its reports.
